title: Strat Chat - How to Check for Understanding
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Brien follows an earlier post on why teachers check for understanding with a short guide to how, within an explicit-teaching approach. He argues that consistency and effectiveness with a few strategies matter more than breadth, and walks through six: true or false questions, multiple choice, think-pair-share, cold calling, mini whiteboards and choral response. Each entry includes a practical caution under a Teacher beware heading, and nearly all hinge on tight routines such as simultaneous reveals and countdowns. He defends strategies often misunderstood, noting that a run of around seven true or false items reduces guessing and that cold calling should be non-random and never used for behaviour management. Mini whiteboards are named the gold standard for making thinking visible. It is a concise practitioner list with clear mechanics, resting on his own experience and a recalled Daisy Christodoulou session more than on cited research.
points: Choosing a few checking strategies and executing them consistently is the core recommendation, since the strategies overlap when used well.
A run of about seven true or false items, answered simultaneously, makes the format resistant to guessing.
Multiple choice items can double as hinge questions when distractors are built from common misconceptions.
Cold calling is reframed as non-random selection of a student who already has an answer ready, with no use for discipline.
Every strategy depends on explicit routines for how students respond, reveal and put materials away.
quotes: There are countless different strategies you could use to check for understanding, however what is most important is that you do a few of them with a high level of consistency and effectiveness. There is also a lot of overlap between these strategies when they’re used well as we are able to use the strengths of each to extend our reach within the class and truly make thinking visible.

Teachers tend to avoid asking true or false questions as they have the perception of being too easy to guess. I attended a professional learning with Daisy Christodoulou where she discussed their practical benefits but only when you use multiple true or false statements at a time to avoid students potentially guessing correctly. My memory of this is that the golden number is to ask around seven true or false questions in a row.

The idea is that they can be used as a hinge question where distractor answers are created from common misconceptions to allow for catching and correcting these misconceptions before they are learned.

Cold calling involves asking a question to the whole class and then selecting a specific student to share their answer with the whole class. This should never be random as we are not trying to set students up for failure.

In my mind this is the gold standard for making thinking visible. It creates a low stakes visible environment where it is easy for the teacher to check and provide feedback with every student in the room.

Teacher beware: processes and routines are key for MWB success. Students need to know how they get their MWB and tools, how they use them, how and when they present their responses, when they can erase their response as well as what to do with their MWB during instruction. Without tight routines your humanities class can very quickly turn into an anatomy class as they doodle.

Asking a question and expecting all students to simultaneously respond after time to think and usually a countdown. This works well on multiple levels as it checks for student recall of recent information within their working memory for a quick, repetitive rehearsal while also ensuring you regain full student attention before you move on to your next point.
